paragraphs.heading: 28.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: Prolactin is a 23-kilodalton (kDa) protein secreted by lactotrophs (also called mammot rophs) that comprise approximately 15–25% of the cells of the anterior pituitary gland [1]. Whereas secretion of other anterior pituitary hormones requires stimulation from the hypo
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: thalamus, lactotrophs exhibit spontaneous prolactin secretion [2]. Prolactin secretion is thus primarily regulated by the inhibitory effect of dopamine neurons in the medial basal hypothalamus, which secrete dopamine at the median eminence of the pituitary into the pituitary portal vessels [2–4]. Factors that either stimulate or inhibit dopamine neurons also inhibit or stimulate prolactin secretion,
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: respectively. Factors that increase prolactin secretion include thyrotropin releasing hor mone (TRH), oxytocin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, estradiol, vasopressin, angiotensin II, serotonin, opioids, and histamine [2]. Alongside dopamine, other factors that decrease prolactin secretion include GABA, acetylcholine, and somatostatin [2]. Prolactin also stimulates dopamine neurons in a “shortloop” feedback mechanism that inhibits fur ther prolactin secretion [2, 3].
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: Prolactin has both tonic and pulsatile secre tion and exhibits a circadian rhythm, with levels highest during sleep and in the early morning hours and lowest a few hours after awakening [2, 5]. Levels also rise slightly after eating [5]. With regard to prolactin levels across the life course, newborns have high prolactin levels at birth, decreasing to within the normal child hood range by 3 months of age [5]. Childhood prolactin levels are similar between males and females before puberty; during puberty, prolac tin levels rise in females, accounting for the higher normal ranges in female adolescents and adults than males [5]. Levels also increase sig nificantly during pregnancy, due at least in part to stimulation by estradiol. By the same mecha nism, prolactin levels may also increase slightly during the preovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle [4]. Suckling and/or nipple stimulation raises prolactin within 1–3 min, with elevations lasting 20–30 min [2], and prolactin levels are elevated during lactation.
paragraphs.heading: and Secretion

paragraphs.text: There are multiple forms of prolactin in circulation: 23 kDa monomeric prolactin; dimeric prolactin, also called “big prolactin;” and macroprolactin, also called “big big pro lactin,” which is over 150 kDa in size and rep resents some combination of prolactin multimers joined by glycosylation and/or immunoglobulin A or immunoglobulin G [3]. Typically, monomeric prolactin comprises approximately 85% of total circulating pro lactin, but some individuals have a predomi nance of big prolactin or macroprolactin [6]. Importantly, dimeric prolactin and macropro lactin have minimal biological activity, but all forms may be measured in immunoassay.
Key actions of prolactin include promoting the differentiation and proliferation of mam mary cells and, during lactation, increasing

milk production [1]. Additionally, prolactin suppresses gonadotropins (luteinizing hormone [LH] and follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]) with a putative mechanism of inhibitory prolac tin signaling at kisspeptin (KNDy) neurons resulting in reduced GnRH [1, 4]. Metabolic effects of prolactin, beyond the scope of this chapter, are also increasingly appreciated [1].

Prolactin levels rise with sleep, exercise, coitus, and both physical and psychological stress. Stress—including the stress of venipunc ture—is a common cause of benign elevations in prolactin. To assess the effect of venipunc ture on prolactin levels, multiple studies have assessed “cannulated prolactin levels,” achieved via intravenous catheter (IV) place ment and serial measurement of prolactin at baseline and periodic intervals over the next two or more hours. These studies report two important findings: (1) on average, prolactin levels decline as time from venipuncture increases, and (2) a large percentage of indi viduals with elevated baseline prolactin levels have normal prolactin after 2 h [7, 8]. For example, in a large cohort of adult women referred for infertility and found to have ele vated prolactin levels on two occasions, 61% had normal 2-h prolactin values, including 5 of 11 women with initial prolactin values above 47 ng/mL (1000 mIU/L) [8]. In a differ ent cohort of 235 men and women referred for hyperprolactinemia with initial values up to 260 ng/mL (5500 mIU/L), 17% of adults had a normal baseline repeat sample, and an addi tional 9% had a normal 2-h “resting” prolac tin [7]. In this cohort, the reduction in prolactin between baseline and 2-h ranged from 2.1 to 35.3 ng/mL (44–749 mIU/L), and, among the female participants, an initial referral prolactin value of 96.2 ng/mL (2040 mU/L) had 97% specificity to detect true hyperprolactinemia [7]. Although similar studies in children are not present in the litera ture, children may also have elevated prolactin due to stress of venipuncture, and placing an

paragraphs.text: IV to draw prolactin after 90–120 min may be a helpful step in the diagnostic process.
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Another important physiologic cause of apparent hyperprolactinemia is “macropro lactinemia,” or an overabundance of circulat ing macroprolactin, which has little biological effect but raises measured prolactin. Assays can differentiate between macroprolactin and monomeric prolactin using either size exclu sion gel filtration chromatography (GFC, the gold standard) or the quicker method of poly ethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, which precipitates out the macroprolactin along with a small percentage of monomeric prolac tin [9]. If ≤40% of total prolactin remains as monomeric prolactin following PEG precipi tation, macroprolactinemia is confirmed [9]. Macroprolactinemia can coexist with patho logic elevations in monomeric prolactin, such that the diagnosis of benign macroprolac tinemia requires both precipitation of ≥60% immunoreactive prolactin and normalization of remaining monomeric prolactin levels fol lowing PEG precipitation [9]. Additionally, the presence of macroprolactin varies over time within individuals [10], so measurement of macroprolactin may need to be repeated in patients with changing clinical circumstances, such as an individual who previously had macroprolactinemia and newly presents with increasing prolactin elevation and/or new symptoms consistent with hyperprolac tinemia. The 2011 Endocrine Society guide lines recommend checking for macroprolactin in those who are asymptomatic [6]. Individuals with benign macroprolactinemia may also have nonspecific symptoms that could be attributed to hyperprolactinemia, such that clinicians may also want to assess for macrop rolactin if symptoms are nonspecific. Because of the substantial overlap between symptoms in those with true monomeric hyperprolac tinemia and benign macroprolactinemia, the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists recommends consideration of macroprolactin measurement in any clini cal situation with possible inconsistencies between labs, symptoms, imaging findings, and/or response to treatment [9]. At present, there are insufficient data in the pediatric pop ulation to guide a specific pediatric recom
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: mendation regarding testing for macroprolactin, and we typically send it in asymptomatic cases and also in those cases with inconsistencies or nonspecific symptoms.
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Several medications antagonize dopamine and thereby increase serum prolactin. Medication-induced hyperprolactinemia is most common with certain atypical antipsy chotics, with risperidone causing the largest elevations, up to 200–250 ng/mL (4255–5319 mIU/L), and paliperidone and olanzapine potentially causing more modest elevations [11]. Among the other atypical anti psychotics, aripiprazole tends to lower prolac tin, whereas quetiapine and lurasidone have minimal effect on prolactin levels [11]. Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and chlor promazine can also raise prolactin, although not typically to the degree that risperidone does [12, 13]. The antiemetic metoclopramide also raises prolactin, potentially up to 200–250 ng/mL (4225–5319 mIU/L) [14].
paragraphs.heading: Prolactin

paragraphs.text: Several other medications may increase prolactin modestly, as described below, but patients with significant prolactin elevations who also happen to be receiving these medica tions should undergo full evaluation for alter native causes of hyperprolactinemia. There are suggestions in the literature that tricyclic anti depressants and monoamine oxidase inhibi tors may cause modest elevations in serum prolactin, but evidence is scant and conflicting [12]. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may also increase prolactin slightly, although these effects are not clinically rele vant in most patients. SSRIs have been reported to cause frank hyperprolactinemia in some individuals, although routine monitoring of prolactin levels is not necessary with SSRI administration [12, 15]. Other medications that may cause mild elevations in prolactin include antihypertensives (verapamil, methyl dopa, and reserpine), opiates, cocaine, and estrogens [12]. Oral contraceptives with rela tively higher doses of ethinyl estradiol could potentially cause mild elevations in prolactin,
paragraphs.heading: Prolactin

paragraphs.text: although there is no definitive evidence that this occurs. A study of transgender women suggests no effect of estradiol treatment on serum prolactin [16], and studies of physio logic hormone replacement with estrogens also do not support an effect on prolactin [12].
paragraphs.heading: Prolactin

paragraphs.text: The most common cause of hyperprolac tinemia in children is prolactinoma [17]. A prolactinoma is an adenoma comprised of pituitary lactotrophs that excessively synthe size and secrete prolactin. Prolactinomas are divided by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (≥10 mm). Females are more likely to present with prolactinoma than males, and the most common time of pediatric presentation is adolescence [18, 19]. Other sel lar or suprasellar lesions can also cause hyper prolactinemia through compression of the pituitary stalk. Hyperprolactinemia due to “stalk effect” most commonly occurs in chil dren with craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, or large pituitary macroadenomas, although this effect can be seen with any mass or infil trative process that compromises the pituitary stalk. Of note, serum prolactin in children with stalk compression from a mass that is not a prolactinoma typically has prolactin levels below 100 ng/mL (2128 mIU/L), in contrast to the much higher levels seen in prolactinomas. Hyperprolactinemia can also be seen in rapidonset obesity with hypothalamic dysfunction, hypoventilation, autonomic dysfunction syn drome (ROHHAD), septo-optic dysplasia, or pituitary stalk interruption [20].
paragraphs.heading: of Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Another pathological cause of hyperpro lactinemia is severe primary hypothyroidism, in which elevated TRH stimulates prolactin secretion. Chronic kidney disease may also cause hyperprolactinemia through both increased prolactin secretion and reduced pro lactin clearance [21]. Serum prolactin is also elevated in patients with advanced liver disease, presumably due to multifactorial etiology, although substantial elevations in prolactin in patients with liver disease still require evalua

tion for other causes [22, 23]. Chest wall trau mas, including burns, other chest injuries, and mastectomy, also raise serum prolactin, pre sumably through the same neural stimulation by which suckling increases prolactin [24]. There is discussion in the literature regarding whether mild elevations in prolactin occur in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [25]. Given the risks of missing primary hyperprolac tinemia as a cause of oligomenorrhea in this population, the presence of PCOS should not preclude full evaluation of patients for other causes of prolactin elevation.

paragraphs.text: For children who present with one elevated prolactin value, the first step is usually to con firm prolactin elevation with repeat testing. Although guidelines in adults recommend that a single elevated value is enough to con firm hyperprolactinemia [6], our practice is
paragraphs.heading: with Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: nearly always to repeat the level in children given the possible effects of stress as well as numerous assay considerations including tim ing of the blood draw, possibility of macrop rolactinemia, and need to assess for “hook effect”. Drawing prolactin in the morning, fasting, avoids the mild elevations in prolactin that may occur with eating and standardizes timing at a nadir of the circadian rhythm of prolactin. It is also good practice to request serial dilutions to exclude the “hook effect,” which is an artifact related to the prolactin immunoassay process by which very high serum prolactin actually causes lower assay results. We find it helpful to assess for hook effect on initial evaluation, and in most cases, it is not present and is not required in further prolactin testing. In children with mild eleva tions in prolactin and/or no signs or symp toms related to hyperprolactinemia, sending a macroprolactin level is also helpful. Additionally, clinicians should consider the possibility of a cannulated prolactin, for which an IV is placed and the prolactin level is drawn 90–120 min after placement to exclude possible elevations due to phlebotomy-related stress.
paragraphs.heading: with Hyperprolactinemia

paragraphs.text: Additional laboratory evaluation should include assessment of TSH, creatinine, and liver function tests, to exclude primary hypo thyroidism, renal disease, and liver disease as causes, respectfully. When clinically applica ble, urine or serum HCG should be sent to assess for pregnancy. Gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and relevant gonadal steroids should be sent to assess for hypogonadism caused by hyperprolactinemia. IGF-1 level may also be useful to assess for the possibility of a GH and prolactin co-secreting tumor. Evaluation of other pituitary axes can also be performed at this time in patients with significant prolac tin elevations, although such testing may not be necessary for those with mild elevations until after MRI results are known.

Once hyperprolactinemia is confirmed on repeat testing, subsequent evaluation depends on the degree of prolactin elevation and the clinical context. For example, children taking a medication that could explain their degree of prolactin elevation can be followed conser vatively if they have a normal pretreatment

prolactin value and are not having any signs or symptoms related to hyperprolactinemia. In the absence of a documented pretreatment prolactin that was normal, clinicians may want to consider the possibility of withdraw ing or substituting the offending drug, if pos sible, versus proceeding with an evaluation to exclude other causes of hyperprolactinemia. Asymptomatic children with minimally ele vated prolactin levels can also be followed conservatively, with consideration of cannu lated prolactin versus serial clinical and labo ratory follow-ups. Beyond these two scenarios, most children with persistently elevated pro lactin generally require magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain using pituitary protocol, with 1 mm cuts and use of a gadolinium-based contrast agent. MRI results will typically guide further evaluation and management, as those without lesions can be followed conservatively and those with sellar or suprasellar lesions will be managed accord ingly. Patients whose MRIs show macroade nomas that may be abutting or compromising the optic chiasm should be referred for visual field testing, as neurosurgical involvement and potentially more aggressive treatment are warranted in cases with visual field impair ment.

Goals of therapy in patients with prolacti noma include (1) reduction of prolactin to a level that alleviates symptoms and permits normal functioning of the hypothalamicpituitary-gonadal axis and (2) stability or reduction of tumor size. Dopamine agonists are the first-line treatment for most prolacti nomas. Appropriate treatment differs depend ing on the size of the prolactinoma and the degree of symptomatology. Patients with microprolactinomas, modest prolactin eleva tions, and few or no symptoms may benefit most from observation, gonadal steroid replacement, or dopamine agonist therapy [6]. Patients with more significant elevations in prolactin and/or larger tumors will require
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: dopamine agonist therapy, and patients with aggressive tumors and/or visual field compro mise may also require surgery or radiotherapy. At the time of this writing, pediatric-specific guidelines for the management of prolacti noma are not published, and adult guidelines are cited as relevant below [6].
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Patients with microprolactinoma, modest prolactin elevations, and no or minimal symp toms may not require medical therapy. Although the natural history of untreated macroprolactinoma is not well-described in children, adult data suggest that microprolac tinomas have a relatively benign course, some times resolving without treatment and rarely progressing [6, 26]. For this reason, children with asymptomatic microprolactinomas can be observed without therapy, with serial pro lactin measurements and MRI. Similarly, for those with microprolactinoma complicated only by hypogonadism, gonadal steroid replacement can be used instead of dopamine agonists as long as immediate fertility is not desired [6]. Of note, these strategies are evidence-based in adults [6], but are not welldescribed in the pediatric literature, nor are there head-to-head comparisons of dopamine agonist therapy versus more conservative treatments in children.
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Dopamine agonists used for the treatment of prolactinomas include cabergoline, bro mocriptine, and, where available, quinagolide. At the time of this writing, the first-line dopa mine agonist is generally cabergoline, which has proven both more effective and better tol erated than bromocriptine in adults [6, 27–33]. Although cabergoline does not have regula tory approval by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the pediatric age group (<18y), we and others routinely use cabergoline as first-line therapy in children, and multiple reports in the literature support use and efficacy in this age group [18–20]. Starting doses of cabergoline are 0.25–0.5 mg/ week, given once or twice weekly, and the majority of patients will achieve normaliza tion of prolactin on these doses [20]. Cabergoline doses are titrated to achieve nor mal prolactin and can be increased up to 3 mg/week, with doses higher than 3 mg potentially effective in select cases [18, 19, 34,
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: 35]. Dopamine agonists at high doses can cause valvular abnormalities, and echocar diography at baseline and follow-up may be warranted for patients requiring higher doses of cabergoline [6].
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Prolactin levels should be repeated within 1 month after starting dopamine agonist ther apy and serially thereafter based on clinical context [6]. Patients with macroprolactinomas should have a repeat MRI within 3 months, whereas an initial interval of 6–12 months is likely appropriate for those with microprolac tinomas [6]. Clinicians should titrate dopa mine agonist therapy to normalize prolactin and perform serial MRIs at intervals of 3–12 months as needed to ensure stability or shrinkage of the prolactinoma. In patients with microprolactinomas for whom prolactin normalizes and the adenoma decreases or resolves over time, tapering and eventual dis continuation of dopamine agonist may be appropriate [6], although, again, data are scant in the pediatric age group. Patients with macroadenomas also typically achieve longterm biochemical and tumor control with dopamine agonists, and the dosage can be titrated to maintain normal prolactin and control of adenoma size.
paragraphs.heading: with Prolactinoma

paragraphs.text: Patients who have visual field compromise and/or who do not achieve control with maxi mal doses of dopamine agonist require man agement by a multidisciplinary team that includes neurosurgery and neuroophthalmol ogy. Cabergoline may still be the appropriate first-line therapy for those presenting with visual field compromise, although we recom mend involvement of neurosurgery and neur oophthalmology from diagnosis for close monitoring and, if the visual field defect does not resolve with dopamine agonists, timely TSS. TSS is the appropriate second-line ther apy for those who cannot tolerate required doses of dopamine agonist or those whose tumor is refractory to treatment [6]. Adjunctive radiotherapy and/or temozolamide may also be necessary in rare cases of aggressive pro lactinoma [33].

Factors that increase prolactin secretion include thyrotropin releasing hor mone (TRH), oxytocin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, estradiol, vasopressin, angiotensin II, serotonin, opioids, and histamine [2]. Alongside dopamine, other factors that decrease prolactin secretion include GABA, acetylcholine, and somatostatin [2]. Prolactin also stimulates dopamine neurons in a “shortloop” feedback mechanism that inhibits fur ther prolactin secretion [2, 3]. Prolactin has both tonic and pulsatile secre tion and exhibits a circadian rhythm, with levels highest during sleep and in the early morning hours and lowest a few hours after awakening [2, 5]. Levels also rise slightly after eating [5]. With regard to prolactin levels across the life course, newborns have high prolactin levels at birth, decreasing to within the normal child hood range by 3 months of age [5]. Childhood prolactin levels are similar between males and females before puberty; during puberty, prolac tin levels rise in females, accounting for the higher normal ranges in female adolescents and adults than males [5]. Levels also increase sig nificantly during pregnancy, due at least in part to stimulation by estradiol. By the same mecha nism, prolactin levels may also increase slightly during the preovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle [4]. Suckling and/or nipple stimulation raises prolactin within 1–3 min, with elevations lasting 20–30 min [2], and prolactin levels are elevated during lactation. ### 28 There are multiple forms of prolactin in circulation: 23 kDa monomeric prolactin; dimeric prolactin, also called “big prolactin;” and macroprolactin, also called “big big pro lactin,” which is over 150 kDa in size and rep resents some combination of prolactin multimers joined by glycosylation and/or immunoglobulin A or immunoglobulin G [3]. Typically, monomeric prolactin comprises approximately 85% of total circulating pro lactin, but some individuals have a predomi nance of big prolactin or macroprolactin [6]. Importantly, dimeric prolactin and macropro lactin have minimal biological activity, but all forms may be measured in immunoassay. Key actions of prolactin include promoting the differentiation and proliferation of mam mary cells and, during lactation, increasing milk production [1]. Additionally, prolactin suppresses gonadotropins (luteinizing hormone [LH] and follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]) with a putative mechanism of inhibitory prolac tin signaling at kisspeptin (KNDy) neurons resulting in reduced GnRH [1, 4]. Metabolic effects of prolactin, beyond the scope of this chapter, are also increasingly appreciated [1]. ### 28.3 Physiologic Causes ### of Hyperprolactinemia Prolactin levels rise with sleep, exercise, coitus, and both physical and psychological stress. Stress—including the stress of venipunc ture—is a common cause of benign elevations in prolactin. To assess the effect of venipunc ture on prolactin levels, multiple studies have assessed “cannulated prolactin levels,” achieved via intravenous catheter (IV) place ment and serial measurement of prolactin at baseline and periodic intervals over the next two or more hours. These studies report two important findings: (1) on average, prolactin levels decline as time from venipuncture increases, and (2) a large percentage of indi viduals with elevated baseline prolactin levels have normal prolactin after 2 h [7, 8]. For example, in a large cohort of adult women referred for infertility and found to have ele vated prolactin levels on two occasions, 61% had normal 2-h prolactin values, including 5 of 11 women with initial prolactin values above 47 ng/mL (1000 mIU/L) [8]. In a differ ent cohort of 235 men and women referred for hyperprolactinemia with initial values up to 260 ng/mL (5500 mIU/L), 17% of adults had a normal baseline repeat sample, and an addi tional 9% had a normal 2-h “resting” prolac tin [7]. In this cohort, the reduction in prolactin between baseline and 2-h ranged from 2.1 to 35.3 ng/mL (44–749 mIU/L), and, among the female participants, an initial referral prolactin value of 96.2 ng/mL (2040 mU/L) had 97% specificity to detect true hyperprolactinemia [7]. Although similar studies in children are not present in the litera ture, children may also have elevated prolactin due to stress of venipuncture, and placing an ## PDF page 784 | printed page 781 IV to draw prolactin after 90–120 min may be a helpful step in the diagnostic process. Another important physiologic cause of apparent hyperprolactinemia is “macropro lactinemia,” or an overabundance of circulat ing macroprolactin, which has little biological effect but raises measured prolactin. Assays can differentiate between macroprolactin and monomeric prolactin using either size exclu sion gel filtration chromatography (GFC, the gold standard) or the quicker method of poly ethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation, which precipitates out the macroprolactin along with a small percentage of monomeric prolac tin [9]. If ≤40% of total prolactin remains as monomeric prolactin following PEG precipi tation, macroprolactinemia is confirmed [9]. Macroprolactinemia can coexist with patho logic elevations in monomeric prolactin, such that the diagnosis of benign macroprolac tinemia requires both precipitation of ≥60% immunoreactive prolactin and normalization of remaining monomeric prolactin levels fol lowing PEG precipitation [9]. Additionally, the presence of macroprolactin varies over time within individuals [10], so measurement of macroprolactin may need to be repeated in patients with changing clinical circumstances, such as an individual who previously had macroprolactinemia and newly presents with increasing prolactin elevation and/or new symptoms consistent with hyperprolac tinemia. The 2011 Endocrine Society guide lines recommend checking for macroprolactin in those who are asymptomatic [6]. Individuals with benign macroprolactinemia may also have nonspecific symptoms that could be attributed to hyperprolactinemia, such that clinicians may also want to assess for macrop rolactin if symptoms are nonspecific. Because of the substantial overlap between symptoms in those with true monomeric hyperprolac tinemia and benign macroprolactinemia, the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists recommends consideration of macroprolactin measurement in any clini cal situation with possible inconsistencies between labs, symptoms, imaging findings, and/or response to treatment [9]. At present, there are insufficient data in the pediatric pop ulation to guide a specific pediatric recom mendation regarding testing for macroprolactin, and we typically send it in asymptomatic cases and also in those cases with inconsistencies or nonspecific symptoms. ### 28.4 Medications that Raise ### Prolactin Several medications antagonize dopamine and thereby increase serum prolactin. Medication-induced hyperprolactinemia is most common with certain atypical antipsy chotics, with risperidone causing the largest elevations, up to 200–250 ng/mL (4255–5319 mIU/L), and paliperidone and olanzapine potentially causing more modest elevations [11]. Among the other atypical anti psychotics, aripiprazole tends to lower prolac tin, whereas quetiapine and lurasidone have minimal effect on prolactin levels [11]. Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and chlor promazine can also raise prolactin, although not typically to the degree that risperidone does [12, 13]. The antiemetic metoclopramide also raises prolactin, potentially up to 200–250 ng/mL (4225–5319 mIU/L) [14]. Several other medications may increase prolactin modestly, as described below, but patients with significant prolactin elevations who also happen to be receiving these medica tions should undergo full evaluation for alter native causes of hyperprolactinemia. There are suggestions in the literature that tricyclic anti depressants and monoamine oxidase inhibi tors may cause modest elevations in serum prolactin, but evidence is scant and conflicting [12]. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may also increase prolactin slightly, although these effects are not clinically rele vant in most patients. SSRIs have been reported to cause frank hyperprolactinemia in some individuals, although routine monitoring of prolactin levels is not necessary with SSRI administration [12, 15]. Other medications that may cause mild elevations in prolactin include antihypertensives (verapamil, methyl dopa, and reserpine), opiates, cocaine, and estrogens [12]. Oral contraceptives with rela tively higher doses of ethinyl estradiol could potentially cause mild elevations in prolactin, ## PDF page 785 | printed page 782 although there is no definitive evidence that this occurs. A study of transgender women suggests no effect of estradiol treatment on serum prolactin [16], and studies of physio logic hormone replacement with estrogens also do not support an effect on prolactin [12]. ### 28.5 Pathologic Causes ### of Hyperprolactinemia The most common cause of hyperprolac tinemia in children is prolactinoma [17]. A prolactinoma is an adenoma comprised of pituitary lactotrophs that excessively synthe size and secrete prolactin. Prolactinomas are divided by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (≥10 mm). Females are more likely to present with prolactinoma than males, and the most common time of pediatric presentation is adolescence [18, 19]. Other sel lar or suprasellar lesions can also cause hyper prolactinemia through compression of the pituitary stalk. Hyperprolactinemia due to “stalk effect” most commonly occurs in chil dren with craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, or large pituitary macroadenomas, although this effect can be seen with any mass or infil trative process that compromises the pituitary stalk. Of note, serum prolactin in children with stalk compression from a mass that is not a prolactinoma typically has prolactin levels below 100 ng/mL (2128 mIU/L), in contrast to the much higher levels seen in prolactinomas. Hyperprolactinemia can also be seen in rapidonset obesity with hypothalamic dysfunction, hypoventilation, autonomic dysfunction syn drome (ROHHAD), septo-optic dysplasia, or pituitary stalk interruption [20]. ### 28 Another pathological cause of hyperpro lactinemia is severe primary hypothyroidism, in which elevated TRH stimulates prolactin secretion. Chronic kidney disease may also cause hyperprolactinemia through both increased prolactin secretion and reduced pro lactin clearance [21]. Serum prolactin is also elevated in patients with advanced liver disease, presumably due to multifactorial etiology, although substantial elevations in prolactin in patients with liver disease still require evalua tion for other causes [22, 23]. Chest wall trau mas, including burns, other chest injuries, and mastectomy, also raise serum prolactin, pre sumably through the same neural stimulation by which suckling increases prolactin [24]. There is discussion in the literature regarding whether mild elevations in prolactin occur in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [25]. Given the risks of missing primary hyperprolac tinemia as a cause of oligomenorrhea in this population, the presence of PCOS should not preclude full evaluation of patients for other causes of prolactin elevation. ### 28.6 Evaluation of Patients ### with Hyperprolactinemia 28.2 ## PDF page 786 | printed page 783 Table 28.2 Evaluation of hyperprolactinemia History – Review of medications – Assessment for signs/symptoms of pubertal delay or altered growth and galactorrhea – Menstrual history and assessment of libido and sexual function when applicable – Assessment for signs/symptoms of mass effect including headaches, visual changes, vomiting – Family history of hyperparathyroidism or pituitary adenomas Physical Examination – Thorough and with special attention to visual field exam, assessment of gynecomastia in males, careful pubertal staging. Drawing prolactin in the morning, fasting, avoids the mild elevations in prolactin that may occur with eating and standardizes timing at a nadir of the circadian rhythm of prolactin. It is also good practice to request serial dilutions to exclude the “hook effect,” which is an artifact related to the prolactin immunoassay process by which very high serum prolactin actually causes lower assay results. We find it helpful to assess for hook effect on initial evaluation, and in most cases, it is not present and is not required in further prolactin testing. When clinically applica ble, urine or serum HCG should be sent to assess for pregnancy. Gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and relevant gonadal steroids should be sent to assess for hypogonadism caused by hyperprolactinemia. For example, children taking a medication that could explain their degree of prolactin elevation can be followed conser vatively if they have a normal pretreatment prolactin value and are not having any signs or symptoms related to hyperprolactinemia. In the absence of a documented pretreatment prolactin that was normal, clinicians may want to consider the possibility of withdraw ing or substituting the offending drug, if pos sible, versus proceeding with an evaluation to exclude other causes of hyperprolactinemia. Dopamine agonists are the first-line treatment for most prolacti nomas. Appropriate treatment differs depend ing on the size of the prolactinoma and the degree of symptomatology. Patients with microprolactinomas, modest prolactin eleva tions, and few or no symptoms may benefit most from observation, gonadal steroid replacement, or dopamine agonist therapy [6]. Patients with more significant elevations in prolactin and/or larger tumors will require ## PDF page 788 | printed page 785 dopamine agonist therapy, and patients with aggressive tumors and/or visual field compro mise may also require surgery or radiotherapy. At the time of this writing, pediatric-specific guidelines for the management of prolacti noma are not published, and adult guidelines are cited as relevant below [6]. Patients with microprolactinoma, modest prolactin elevations, and no or minimal symp toms may not require medical therapy. Although the natural history of untreated macroprolactinoma is not well-described in children, adult data suggest that microprolac tinomas have a relatively benign course, some times resolving without treatment and rarely progressing [6, 26]. For this reason, children with asymptomatic microprolactinomas can be observed without therapy, with serial pro lactin measurements and MRI. Similarly, for those with microprolactinoma complicated only by hypogonadism, gonadal steroid replacement can be used instead of dopamine agonists as long as immediate fertility is not desired [6]. Of note, these strategies are evidence-based in adults [6], but are not welldescribed in the pediatric literature, nor are there head-to-head comparisons of dopamine agonist therapy versus more conservative treatments in children. Dopamine agonists used for the treatment of prolactinomas include cabergoline, bro mocriptine, and, where available, quinagolide. At the time of this writing, the first-line dopa mine agonist is generally cabergoline, which has proven both more effective and better tol erated than bromocriptine in adults [6, 27–33]. Although cabergoline does not have regula tory approval by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the pediatric age group (<18y), we and others routinely use cabergoline as first-line therapy in children, and multiple reports in the literature support use and efficacy in this age group [18–20]. Starting doses of cabergoline are 0.25–0.5 mg/ week, given once or twice weekly, and the majority of patients will achieve normaliza tion of prolactin on these doses [20]. Cabergoline doses are titrated to achieve nor mal prolactin and can be increased up to 3 mg/week, with doses higher than 3 mg potentially effective in select cases [18, 19, 34, 35]. Dopamine agonists at high doses can cause valvular abnormalities, and echocar diography at baseline and follow-up may be warranted for patients requiring higher doses of cabergoline [6]. Prolactin levels should be repeated within 1 month after starting dopamine agonist ther apy and serially thereafter based on clinical context [6]. Patients with macroprolactinomas should have a repeat MRI within 3 months, whereas an initial interval of 6–12 months is likely appropriate for those with microprolac tinomas [6]. Clinicians should titrate dopa mine agonist therapy to normalize prolactin and perform serial MRIs at intervals of 3–12 months as needed to ensure stability or shrinkage of the prolactinoma. In patients with microprolactinomas for whom prolactin normalizes and the adenoma decreases or resolves over time, tapering and eventual dis continuation of dopamine agonist may be appropriate [6], although, again, data are scant in the pediatric age group. Patients with macroadenomas also typically achieve longterm biochemical and tumor control with dopamine agonists, and the dosage can be titrated to maintain normal prolactin and control of adenoma size. Patients who have visual field compromise and/or who do not achieve control with maxi mal doses of dopamine agonist require man agement by a multidisciplinary team that includes neurosurgery and neuroophthalmol ogy. Cabergoline may still be the appropriate first-line therapy for those presenting with visual field compromise, although we recom mend involvement of neurosurgery and neur oophthalmology from diagnosis for close monitoring and, if the visual field defect does not resolve with dopamine agonists, timely TSS. TSS is the appropriate second-line ther apy for those who cannot tolerate required doses of dopamine agonist or those whose tumor is refractory to treatment [6]. Adjunctive radiotherapy and/or temozolamide may also be necessary in rare cases of aggressive pro lactinoma [33]. Other important considerations in the management of prolactinomas in children include evaluating the possibility of a genetic etiology and screening for bone health.
